PODCAST: Love Like a Mother

by Sheila Wray Gregoire | Sep 3, 2026 | Parenting Young Kids, Podcasts | 7 comments

Have you ever felt like God was more like some than others?

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 82:17
Instaread

When you’re a woman, and God is always talked about as male, it can make it seem like God can understand men more than women. Like the things that women go through are a little alien to God, more so than the things men go through.

I remember when I first started reading about how God doesn’t actually have a gender (something that even John Piper believes!), and I started crying thinking that God understood cramps. I know it  sounds silly, but it always seemed like, as a woman, I was separate from God in a way that my husband wasn’t.

And so I just loved Elizabeth Berget’s book Love Like a Mother: How the Sacred Work of Motherhood Reveals the Heart of God. She takes us through all the different ways in Scripture that God is referred to as a mother, and spoken of in mothering terms, so many of which I completely missed! And in the work of pregnancy, labour, sleepless nights, etc., Elizabeth shows that these are all things that actually help us reveal God’s heart even more. This is a beautiful book, and so healing! I think you’ll love this conversation.

23:09 What Women’s Bodies Can Teach Us About God & Christ’s Sacrifice on the Cross
33:13 Grief, Miscarriage, & Infertility – Illuminating God’s Longing, Grief, & Enduring Love
40:19 God as Shekinah – Like a Mother Who Protects Us & Stays With Us
46:05 Mental Load, Toddlers, & God’s Patience – Jesus Understands “I Need a Minute”

58:45 Breath Prayers for Real Life: A Simple Spiritual Practice for Busy Seasons
01:00:38 Conclusion: How to Connect With Elizabeth Berget

Check it out!

Key Talking Points

1. Scripture gives us a much bigger picture of God than we often hear in church.

Elizabeth’s argument isn’t that Christians should stop calling God Father. Rather, Scripture uses many images for God—including maternal ones—and ignoring those images can leave women working harder to recognize themselves in the biblical picture of God.

2. God’s compassion has a distinctly maternal dimension.

Exploring the Hebrew connection between God’s compassion and the word for womb can suggest a picture of God whose care is visceral, protective, and deeply responsive—like a mother instinctively responding when her child is in distress.

3. Motherhood is not supposed to be a spiritual performance.

God understands what exhaustion actually feels like. Mothers of young children aren’t failing spiritually because they can’t maintain elaborate devotional routines; God can meet them in the ordinary, chaotic work of caring for their children.

4. Women’s embodied experiences can become theological lenses.

Pregnancy, birth, breastfeeding, vulnerability, physical exhaustion, and even the ways women’s bodies are permanently changed through motherhood can help illuminate biblical descriptions of God’s love. Rather than being obstacles to theology, women’s bodies and experiences can help us know God more fully.

5. God’s love is both sacrificial and life-giving—but not a call to martyrdom.

Connections can be drawn between childbirth, Christ’s suffering, and the language of “this is my body, broken for you,” while also emphasizing an important boundary: God does not ask mothers to completely erase themselves. Rest, nourishment, health, and bodily care matter to God too.

6. God’s protection can mean presence, not just rescue.

The discussion of Shekinah offers a compelling distinction between God protecting us by delivering us from danger and God protecting us by remaining present with us when the danger doesn’t disappear. Sometimes God’s care looks less like removing the darkness and more like refusing to leave us alone in it.

7. Rest is not a failure of faith.

Let’s challenge the idea that the harder something is, the more holy it must be. Jesus experienced exhaustion and withdrew from crowds, while Scripture repeatedly portrays God as attentive to our physical needs. Sleep, boundaries, and help from others can be part of faithful living rather than evidence that we’re falling short.

8. Expanding our understanding of God could also expand the church’s understanding of women.

Elizabeth’s larger hope is that churches would stop treating women’s voices and experiences as peripheral and instead recognize that women have theological insight to offer precisely because of their embodied experiences. The result could be a richer theology and a fuller picture of God.

Like, I just remember being I, like you said earlier, a husk of my former self. Like, I couldn’t think, I couldn’t read. I felt like I couldn’t articulate. I, you know, I’d kind of drag us through the days just like praying for nap time. Right. And so I just think there’s such a comfort to knowing that, like, the God who never slumbers or sleeps also came to earth as a human and a limited human body and got tired because there’s so much in the Bible, that indicates that God wants us rested. And I think we’re so quick to paint that in a spiritual frame of like, God wants us resting in him and relying on him. Absolutely. I think God also just wants us to feel good in our bodies, and we’re not going to do that if we’re not sleeping. And so, you know, there’s, I think I always say like, oh, if I had another life, I would, you know, be an immigration attorney or I would do this or that. Right. Like, but I feel like if I had another life, one of my things would be like men and women should be getting up equally in the middle of the night, like, as everybody’s working the next day, even if you’re a stay at home mom. And I think the messaging I got and this was not for my husband, but I just think, like the cultures we both grew up in was, well, he goes to work the next day, so I’m going to be the one to get up. And I was nursing and most of my kids would not take bottles very easily. And so part of it is like, okay, it makes sense. But I was also, you know, I got to a point, I talk about this because, like, I can’t do this another night. I’m literally going crazy and, you know, making my husband deal with it. I put on headphones or earplugs and went into a different part of the house and just was like, good luck. You know, this is after my son was weaned. So, I mean, you know, I wasn’t it wasn’t like, sounds really cruel when I say that. But yeah, I just think we get to a point where we’re so tired and Jesus can so relate with that. And like I said before Isaiah 40:11, God is so gentle to those with young and sees just how tired you are and doesn’t want that for you. It’s not like we’re going to snap our fingers and do it, but it’s like, I think, again, we sometimes get this message that the harder something is, the more holy it is. And so we can sometimes get into this martyr mentality of, well, I got to be the one to get up with this kid every time because this is the most holy option. And it’s like no you’re a body, you’re not God. You’re limited. Like, we need some sleep. We have to figure out a way, get you some sleep, you know. So.

Sheila
Absolutely, absolutely. And I know, you know a couple of times where I was just exhausted and my mom would take the kids so that we could sleep or when Katie was just at the end of her rope with her first, you know, there was one night where I, yeah, I just took her and. Yeah, it’s like you just need that. Yeah. And God does understand that we need rest. I love that. So when you think about how, seeking God as a mother means that women can see themselves in the image of God more, what kind of change do you think that could make? If we could, if we could catch that vision? Like, what are you hoping that people will see with this book?

Elizabeth
Yeah, I think I primarily hope that women and mothers who are weary, physically or otherwise, or feel spiritual shame for not keeping up in kind of those intense seasons of motherhood who are feeling that extra pressure of like, okay, I’m a mom now. I got to get together who are feeling those pressures from, you know, whether it’s their church or ideologies they grew up with I really like my primary prayer is that they feel seen and just so deeply loved that they can get a taste of, okay, as much as I love this little kid so much as I love this little baby in my arms or my grown kid, you know? So God loves me to an even greater degree. Like I am so beloved, even if I’m not keeping up with these spiritual disciplines, even if I lost it at my kids this afternoon, like, you know, no, like no matter what, that God sees them and that they are just deeply beloved as much as they love their own kids. I think that’s my primary hope. And then in terms of broader help. I did pray a lot for people in the midst of things like deconstruction and reconstruction of their faith. And that’s something I’ve experienced. And, I think it can be a really gentle portal back to knowing God, to know God as Mother in addition to father. If you’ve maybe grown up with a punitive or angry picture of God to know some of these scriptures that do really explicitly talk about a maternal care for you from the divine. And so I think I pray that this book can really speak to those who are, who really want to remain Christian, who want to remain, within the faith, but are struggling to know, like, okay, how can I do that in a way that, is not kind of exactly what I grew up with? And then, yeah, just more broadly, I think like, oh, what could change in the church if we really valued the voices and the bodies and the experiences of women? Like what would change? What would change in our theology? What would change in our practice? What would change in the way we love our communities? Like if we didn’t just relegate the voices of women to the sidelines of the nurseries or the potluck kitchens, right? If we said, hey, you and your body and your experiences really can teach us about God, we want to hear from you.
You know, I think, I had my father in law, who is a lifelong evangelical pastor and has a more conservative viewpoint than I do, but is a pretty open minded individual, fantastic grandfather and father in law, like nothing but good to say about this man. But I had him read an early version of this book to say, okay, what are your red flags to someone who’s coming from a complementary space, who’s, you know, maybe, you know, just has a kind of a different view of some of these things than I do.

What’s going to make someone like you put this book down? And he really just said, you know, his response was surprising. He said, there’s nothing in here that’s radical, this is all coming straight from Scripture. But boy, we don’t hear about this a lot in churches like mine, because we don’t give women the microphone and so I would say, like even to those of you in, complementarian circles, like, you know, this doesn’t have to maybe look like a woman giving getting up on a Sunday morning if that’s just something you can’t get behind.
But like, you need to be asking the women in your congregation in your life, like, how do you know God? What is something you know about God that I can’t because I do not have a female body or female experiences? So yeah, I think there’s kind of a broad hope that, you know, across the complementarian and egalitarian spectrum, that churches would just be really open to hearing from women and knowing God through the voices and experiences and bodies of women.

Sheila
Because it is such a tremendous feeling of relief and intimacy with God. I think when you realize that you’re not different.

Elizabeth
And I think I will talk about the work of Bekah Stewart in my book where she, her book Permission to Matter. Oh, the subtitle is not coming to me right now. But she essentially talks about how women have to work so hard often in our church spaces to find themselves in the stories. And she calls it intellectual flexibility, where they’re just, they’re just doing this extra work that men are often not having to do to find themselves in the truths of Scripture, because we’re not often framing it in a very feminine framework or perspective. And so, yeah, I would hope that this, well, kind of helps open a variety of church leaders and, and church goers to think about God in a more expansive way, because not only is it going to help both men and women to know God as mother. I mean, I always say, like, you know, all of us are born needing a mom and maternal care, and that need is best met in God alone, just like every other need we have. And so, not only is it going to, you know, benefit men and women, but I think it’s going to help us have a more full and expansive picture of God that is rooted in Scripture. So and that’s what we’re all after, right? We want to know God. And so I think when we ignore these maternal ideas, we are ignoring half the face of God.

Sheila
Yeah, exactly. Very last thing. I really liked what you did at the end of each chapter where you had those spiritual practices that you were mentioning. But I want to draw attention to breath prayers, because I think for a lot of people that are listening, they haven’t done this. It sounds kind of odd. But I love the concept of it. So can you explain what a breath prayer is?

Elizabeth
Yeah, absolutely. So, a breath prayer is essentially as you breathe in, you say or think or kind of focus on one statement. And then as you breathe out, you focus on another, usually complementarian statement. So I first came across this practice in a book by Brennan Manning where he would say, essentially like, you are God, I am beloved. And you just kind of do that in and out as many times as you can or within a certain set of time. Or if you’re a busy mom and you’re standing at the kitchen sink maybe just once or twice, right? Like, but it’s just this, like, very simple way of tethering yourself to who God is and the truth of God and the truth of your own belovedness wherever you are, you could be in traffic, you could be at work, you could be at church, you could be, you know, trying to get a kid down for a nap for the 18th hour in a row. Right? Like you can do it anywhere. And I think that’s why it can be a really helpful practice, especially for busy moms. And so, yeah, I include a breath prayer at the end of each chapter. That is, you know, kind of connected to the chapter’s contents. Something you can kind of take with you a little spiritual practice, you can tuck in your pocket that’s going to help tether you to the truth of how God is looking out for you, even in those kinds of crazy moments.

Sheila
Because I love that there isn’t going to be anything about how you have to get up an hour before your child.

Elizabeth
Please don’t. So please don’t do that. Especially if you’re not sleeping and if it serves you, if that’s like I always I just feel like I want to say that so clearly. If those spiritual practices are still working with you, great. Amazing. But if they’re not, there are other ways to connect with God in these seasons that are a little bit less demanding.

Sheila
Amen. Okay, so the book, again, is Love Like a Mother – How the Sacred Work of Motherhood Reveals the Maternal Heart of God, by Elizabeth Berget. And I’m going to put the link in the podcast notes where you can find it, and a link to Elizabeth’s Substack. What’s your Substack called again?

Elizabeth
It’s called Back of the flock.

Sheila
Ok. So we’ll put a link to that too. Yeah. Anywhere else people should find you.

Elizabeth
Instagram Elizabeth_A_Berget. And yeah, Substack and my website is just Elizabethberget.com and there’s all kinds of good information on there as well.

Sheila
Great. So thank you for this conversation. That’s been wonderful.

Elizabeth
Thank you. Oh my gosh. This has been a joy. I really appreciate it.
